# Hiring a Web Developer in Armenia: 10 Questions to Ask Before You Sign

URL: https://armenghazaryan.am/blog/hire-web-developer-armenia/
Published: 2026-10-24
Category: Web Development

Choosing a web developer is one of those decisions that feels small until it isn't. A good one gives you a fast, findable website you control. A bad one leaves you with a site you can't edit, a domain registered in someone else's name, and nobody answering the phone.

I've been on the developer side of this conversation with more than 50 clients since 2022. These are the questions I'd want any business in Armenia to ask — including when they're talking to me.

## 1. Can I see live websites you've built?

Not mockups, not Dribbble shots — live URLs you can open on your phone. Check how fast they load, whether they work on mobile, and whether they still exist. A developer's own site is a good signal too.

## 2. Who will own the domain, hosting and code?

This is the most important question on the list. The domain (your `.am` or `.com`) should be registered **in your name**, on an account you can log into. You should own the code and have access to the hosting. If a developer insists on keeping everything under their account, walk away politely.

## 3. What will the site be built with — and why?

There's no single right answer — WordPress, a site builder, or custom code with something like Python and PostgreSQL can all be correct. What matters is that the developer can explain *why* it fits your project, and what it means for cost, speed and future changes.

## 4. How will it perform on mobile?

Most visitors in Armenia will see your site on a phone, often over mobile data. Ask how the developer handles image sizes, loading speed and mobile layouts. Then test the result yourself before final payment.

## 5. Is basic SEO included?

At minimum: proper page titles and descriptions, clean headings, fast loading, a sitemap, `robots.txt`, and connecting the site to Google Search Console. These cost very little during the build and a lot to retrofit.

## 6. How do you handle Armenian, Russian and English?

If you need more than one language, ask how each version gets its own URL and language tags, who translates the content, and how the design copes with longer text. "We'll add a translate button" is not a multilingual strategy.

## 7. Can I edit the content myself?

Ask for a demo of the admin panel or CMS before you sign. If changing a price or a photo requires the developer, you'll pay for that forever. For [Hasmik's Club](https://hasmiksclub.am), for example, the admin panel was a core part of the project — the team runs members and events themselves.

## 8. Have you integrated payments, bookings or a CRM before?

If your site takes money or appointments, you want someone who has done it before and knows how to handle failures, refunds and confirmations. I've built conference registration with online payments ([Epilepsy.am](https://epilepsy.am)) and consultation booking ([Kesoyan.am](https://kesoyan.am)) — ask any developer for their equivalents.

## 9. What's the timeline, and how is payment split?

A professional proposal breaks the work into milestones — for example design, build, content, launch — with payments tied to each. Be wary of 100% upfront, and equally wary of a timeline that sounds too good to be true.

## 10. What happens after launch?

Ask about bug fixes, security updates, backups, and what small changes cost. Agree on how quickly they'll respond if the site goes down. Launch is the start of a website's life, not the end of the project.

## A quick checklist

- Live portfolio sites checked on your phone
- Domain and hosting in your name
- Clear stack choice, explained
- SEO basics and Search Console included
- Multilingual plan if you need it
- Admin panel demoed
- Milestones and payment schedule in writing
- Post-launch support agreed

If you're comparing budgets, my guide on [what actually drives website development costs in Armenia](/blog/website-development-cost-armenia/) pairs well with this list.

## Looking for a web developer?

I'm Armen Ghazaryan — a web developer and Technical Product Owner from Armenia. Ask me all ten questions: [get in touch here](https://armenghazaryan.am/#contact).

Before any job title, I was a developer. Since March 2022 I've worked as a **freelance web developer**, serving 50+ clients across industries and countries, from simple landing pages to full web-app architectures. I manage the whole lifecycle: design, build, SEO and delivery.

# Website Development in Armenia: What Actually Drives the Cost (2026 Guide)

URL: https://armenghazaryan.am/blog/website-development-cost-armenia/
Published: 2026-10-17
Category: Web Development

"How much does a website cost?" is the first question almost every business in Armenia asks me — and the honest answer is "it depends" until we've talked for ten minutes. That's not a dodge. Two sites that look similar on the surface can differ in effort by a factor of ten.

I've built websites and web apps for 50+ clients since 2022, so instead of throwing out a number that won't fit your project, here's what actually moves the price — and how to get a quote you can trust.

## 1. What kind of website you actually need

The single biggest factor is the type of project:

- **Landing page** — one page, one goal (calls, sign-ups, bookings). Fastest to build.
- **Business website** — several pages: services, about, contact, maybe a blog. Most companies in Yerevan start here.
- **Online store** — products, cart, checkout, payments, delivery options, stock. Much more logic and testing.
- **Web application** — anything with user accounts, dashboards, subscriptions or custom workflows. This is software, not a website, and it's priced like software.

Be honest about which one you need today. A great business site that launches in a few weeks usually beats an ambitious platform that's still "almost ready" six months later.

## 2. Template or custom design

A well-chosen template can be adapted quickly. A custom design — your brand, your layout, your interactions — takes design time plus build time. Custom makes sense when your website *is* your product or your main sales channel. For a new business that mostly needs to look credible on Google Maps and Instagram, a polished template is often the smarter spend.

## 3. Languages: Armenian, Russian, English

This one is specific to Armenia and often underestimated. Many businesses here need the site in **Armenian, Russian and English**. Each language means:

- translated and proofread content (not machine-translated menus),
- layouts that survive longer Russian words and Armenian script,
- separate URLs and proper language tags so Google shows the right version to the right visitor.

A trilingual site isn't three times the work, but it's meaningfully more than one language.

## 4. Payments, bookings and other integrations

Every integration adds work and testing:

- **Online payments** — card processing through a payment provider, receipts, failure handling. On [Epilepsy.am](https://epilepsy.am) attendee registration included integrated online payments.
- **Bookings and scheduling** — available slots, confirmations, reminders. [Kesoyan.am](https://kesoyan.am) exists so clients can book consultations without back-and-forth.
- **CRM and email marketing** — sending leads and customers into the tools you already use.
- **Delivery, stock, accounting** — common for online stores.

## 5. An admin panel you can actually use

Who updates the site after launch? If the answer is "us, every week," you need a content-management system or a custom admin panel. [Hasmik's Club](https://hasmiksclub.am), a membership platform I built, is backed by a strong admin panel because the team manages members, events and an e-book library themselves. That's real scope — but it's what stops you paying a developer for every text change.

## 6. SEO, speed and analytics

A website nobody finds is a cost, not an asset. Basic technical SEO — clean HTML, page titles and descriptions, a sitemap, fast loading on mobile, Google Search Console — should be part of any professional build. Content strategy and ongoing SEO are a separate, ongoing piece of work.

## 7. Hosting, domain and maintenance

Budget for the parts after launch: the domain (for example a `.am` domain), hosting, SSL, backups, security updates and small fixes. Ask whether maintenance is included, billed hourly, or not offered at all.

## How to get an accurate quote

Send your developer a short brief with:

1. What the website must achieve (leads, sales, bookings, credibility).
2. The pages or features you need — and which ones can wait for version two.
3. Languages.
4. Integrations: payments, booking, CRM, delivery.
5. Who will update content after launch.
6. Two or three websites you like, and why.
7. Your deadline and a rough budget range.

That last point matters. A budget range isn't a trap — it lets a good developer tell you what's realistic and where to save.
